vignette: Leilani, a 36-year-old urban planner of South Eastern Asian descent, had always been drawn to helping others. Her work as a relief worker in a war-torn country was a natural extension of her compassionate nature. However, it was during one fateful mission that her life took a drastic turn. While delivering aid to a remote village, Leilani's team came under attack. She remembered the sound of gunfire and screams, the smell of smoke and blood, and the feeling of utter chaos. In the aftermath of the incident, Leilani struggled to process what had happened. Old memories began to resurface, and she found herself triggered by seemingly innocuous things – old photos of her time in the war zone, being in natural environments that reminded her of the village, and even the sound of shouting. These triggers would transport her back to that fateful day, and she would feel like she was reliving the horror all over again. As Leilani tried to navigate these intense emotions, she turned to maladaptive strategies to cope. She began to physically harm herself as a way to release overwhelming feelings, believing that the physical pain would distract her from the emotional turmoil. She also tried to push the memories out of her mind, using thought suppression to avoid reliving the trauma. When this didn't work, she turned to mental distraction, keeping her mind occupied at all times with work or other activities. Despite these efforts, Leilani's sense of threat remained ever-present. Flashbacks would occur without warning, and she would find herself suddenly feeling like she was back in the war zone, reacting as if the traumatic experience were happening all over again. Even small movements nearby could startle her, making her react as if she were in danger. At night, she struggled to fall asleep, convinced that she needed to stay alert to protect herself from potential threats. When Leilani tried to recall the events of that day, she was overcome with intense rage. She couldn't explain why – it just felt like a simmering anger that threatened to boil over at any moment. Attempting to put her thoughts into words only made things worse; she would lose the thread of her narrative and be unable to finish. The memory itself felt alien, as if it belonged to someone else rather than to her. As time went on, Leilani's avoidance behaviors began to take a toll on her daily life. She stopped taking her usual walks in the park, afraid of being triggered by the natural environment. She also became withdrawn at work, struggling to focus on her urban planning projects. Her relationship with her partner suffered as well; she felt like she was pushing him away, unable to open up about her experiences. It wasn't until Leilani's partner staged an intervention, expressing concern for her well-being and encouraging her to seek help, that she realized the extent of her struggles. With a deep sense of trepidation, Leilani began seeking therapy, hoping to find a way to reconcile her past with her present. What frightened her most was the prospect of confronting those memories head-on, but what she hoped for was a chance to heal and rebuild – to reclaim her life from the grip of trauma.
